label: The Five Platonic Solids
notes: This chapter, printed pages 148 through 159, builds the five regular polyhedra from inspectable data: vertices, edges, faces, and Schlaefli symbols. We separate three kinds of claim throughout, namely metric, combinatorial, and topological, so each solid is represented both as a visual model and as a count that can fail if the construction is wrong.

label: What Makes a Solid Regular
notes: Regularity is strict. Every face must be one congruent regular polygon, every vertex must look identical, and every edge the same length. The notebook keeps p and q visible because the chapter formulas are really statements about the pair, not about canned mesh assets, so we read regularity as equality of faces, edges, and vertex neighborhoods.

label: The Schlaefli Symbol {p,q}
notes: The symbol packs the whole local rule into two integers. Faces are regular p-gons and exactly q of them meet around each vertex. From this single pair every count and every radius in the chapter follows, which is why we never hide p and q inside a mesh. Read each solid by naming its pair first.

label: Where Four Solids Come From
notes: Four of the five appear inside familiar families. The tetrahedron is a triangular pyramid, the cube is a square prism, the octahedron is a triangular antiprism, and the icosahedron combines a pentagonal antiprism with two pentagonal caps. Inspecting the vertex pattern in each family is a combinatorial check; all three families have Euler characteristic two.

label: Drawings: Net and Schlegel
notes: A solid can be drawn many ways and each drawing keeps different information. A net records faces and fold edges but loses the final angles. A Schlegel diagram projects the vertex-edge graph into the plane and counts the outside as one face. That projection is exactly why Euler's formula can be proved by studying flat planar maps.

label: Euler's Polyhedron Formula
notes: Euler's formula bridges drawing and classification. Build the Schlegel map edge by edge: a new edge to a new vertex raises V and E together, while an edge closing a region raises E and F together. Starting from one vertex and the exterior region, the alternating sum V minus E plus F stays fixed at two throughout.

label: The Counting Relations
notes: Two incidence counts complete the picture. Counting edge-ends at vertices gives qV equals twice E, and counting sides of faces gives pF equals twice E. Each edge is shared by two vertices and two faces, which is the source of both factors of two. Combined with Euler's formula these relations pin down V, E, and F exactly.

label: Why Exactly Five
notes: Solving the counting relations with Euler's formula forces a denominator that must stay positive. That positivity is equivalent to the inequality on p and q shown here, which only the five admissible pairs satisfy. The argument is purely combinatorial: no metric input is needed to prove that the list of regular convex polyhedra closes at five.

label: The Five Solids by Number
notes: Here is the full census. Tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron, with their symbols and their vertex, edge, and face counts. Notice the symmetry of the table: the cube and octahedron swap V with F, as do the dodecahedron and icosahedron, while the tetrahedron sits on its own with four of everything but edges.

label: Duality: Faces Become Vertices
notes: Reciprocation swaps the symbol p with q. A clean computational model places a point at each face center and joins two centers when their faces share an edge, exchanging vertices and faces while keeping the edge count. For a regular solid each reciprocal edge is perpendicular to the original edge it crosses, a fact we test numerically.

label: Radii and the Characteristic Tetrahedron
notes: The metric data is packaged by one right-angled tetrahedron whose corners are a vertex, an edge midpoint, a face center, and the solid's center. From it come three nested spheres: circumradius to a vertex, midradius to an edge midpoint, inradius to a face. The central half-angle and dihedral angle follow from the same right triangles.

label: Euler Is Necessary, Not Sufficient
notes: A closing guardrail. A rectangular box shares the cube's vertex, edge, and face counts and its reciprocal has the octahedral graph, yet it is not regular: edge lengths split into three sizes. So proving only that V minus E plus F equals two does not prove regularity; we must also check equal faces, equal edges, and equal vertex neighborhoods.
